procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Industrial Tribunal directing reinstatement of Respondent 1.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The company filed a writ petition (O.J.C. No. 280 of 1965) in the Orissa High Court seeking to quash the Tribunal's order. The High Court rejected the company's contentions and held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the termination of service of respondent 1 was not in bona fide exercise of the power. The High Court also held that ordinarily the relief against an illegal termination of service was reinstatement though in some cases it may be .considered inexpedient to do so, in which event a suitable compensation would be the proper r~lief. Lastly, it held that the present case was not one of those exceptions to the gerleral rule of re-instatement and the Tribunal having exercised its discretion it could not interfere with the Tribunal's order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on January 27, 1969.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The company applied for special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court granted special leave, but limited it to the question of whether the relief to Respondent 1 should have been reinstatement or compensation. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the order of the Tribunal and the High Court and instead directed the appellant-company to pay to the 1st respondent Rs. 3840 as and by way of compensation.

directions: The order of the Tribunal and the High Court is quashed.
The appellant-company is directed to pay to the 1st respondent Rs. 3840.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Industrial Tribunal was justified in directing reinstatement of a workman whose services were terminated for security reasons, even if the termination was found to be illegal.

facts: A workman's service was terminated by his employer company based on an adverse police security report.
The company felt it was undesirable for security reasons to continue employing the workman.
The Industrial Tribunal found the termination to be illegal and punitive because the report was not disclosed to the workman.
However, the Tribunal also found that the termination was not a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice.
Despite this, the Tribunal ordered the workman's reinstatement with full back wages.
The High Court upheld the Tribunal's order, stating it could not interfere with the Tribunal's exercise of discretion.
law: The normal rule for an illegal or unjustified termination of service is reinstatement.

However, this is not a hard and fast rule. The Tribunal has the discretion to award compensation instead of reinstatement in "unusual or exceptional" cases where reinstatement would be inexpedient or improper.
This discretion must be exercised judicially and not mechanically, based on the specific circumstances of the case.
An exceptional case arises when an employer genuinely loses confidence in an employee on grounds of security, making it hazardous or prejudicial to the industry to retain them.
The High Court has a duty to interfere with a Tribunal's order if the Tribunal has exercised its discretion improperly or without regard to well-settled principles.
application: The Supreme Court found that the company's decision to terminate the workman was based on a genuine apprehension for security, stemming from the adverse police report.
The termination was not due to any unfair labour practice but was a direct result of the company's bona fide belief that it was a security risk to retain the employee.
The Court determined that the employer had genuinely lost confidence in the workman. Forcing the company to re-employ someone it considered a security risk would be prejudicial to its interests.
This situation constituted an "exceptional case" where the general rule of reinstatement should not be applied.
The Court concluded that the Tribunal had exercised its discretion "mechanically" by ordering reinstatement without properly weighing the unique security circumstances.
Similarly, the High Court erred by refusing to interfere, wrongly assuming it could not review the Tribunal's improper exercise of discretion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the lower courts' decisions, holding that the Industrial Tribunal was not justified in ordering reinstatement. The Court reasoned that because the employer had a genuine and bona fide loss of confidence in the workman for security reasons, this was an exceptional case where the appropriate relief was compensation, not reinstatement.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its writ jurisdiction under Article 226, can refuse to interfere with a discretionary order of the Industrial Tribunal on the sole ground that the Tribunal has exercised its discretion.

facts: An Industrial Tribunal ordered the reinstatement of a workman whose service was terminated for security reasons.
The Tribunal has the discretion to award compensation instead of reinstatement in exceptional cases.
The High Court was asked to review this order under its writ jurisdiction (Article 226).
The High Court refused to interfere, reasoning that since the Tribunal had exercised its discretion, the High Court could not intervene.
law: A High Court, exercising its writ jurisdiction under Article 226, has a duty to interfere with a discretionary order of a lower tribunal if that discretion was not exercised properly.
A tribunal must exercise its discretion "judicially and in accordance with well recognised principles."
If a tribunal exercises its discretion in disregard of relevant circumstances or established principles, it is considered a case of "no exercise of discretion or of one not legally exercised."
In such cases, the High Court cannot simply state that discretion was exercised; it must examine the circumstances to see if the exercise was proper.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Industrial Tribunal had exercised its discretion "mechanically without weighing the circumstances of the case," which amounted to "no exercise of discretion at all."
The Supreme Court held that the High Court's refusal to interfere was "equally mechanical and amounted to refusal to exercise its jurisdiction."
By simply accepting the Tribunal's decision on the grounds that it was a discretionary one, the High Court failed to perform its duty of judicial review.
The High Court should have examined whether the Tribunal's discretion was exercised properly and in accordance with legal principles, which it failed to do.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's position, holding that a High Court cannot, under its writ jurisdiction, refuse to interfere with a discretionary order from a tribunal on the sole ground that discretion was exercised. The High Court has a duty to examine whether that discretion was exercised judicially, properly, and in accordance with well-settled principles. A failure to conduct this examination is a refusal to exercise its own jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Industrial Tribunal was justified in directing reinstatement of a workman whose services were terminated for security reasons, even if the termination was found to be illegal.
appellant_arguments: The court should have ordered compensation instead of reinstatement.
The employee worked in a crucial and sensitive area (the blast furnace), and the company could not risk retaining an employee it considered a security risk.
The Tribunal had already found that the termination was not due to the workman's union activities.
respondent_arguments: An employer should not be allowed to terminate an employee based on secret police reports that are not disclosed to the workman or the Tribunal, as this prevents the workman from challenging the basis of the termination.
Allowing termination based on undisclosed reports would enable an employer to dismiss a workman under the pretext of being a security danger.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its writ jurisdiction under Article 226, can refuse to interfere with a discretionary order of the Industrial Tribunal on the sole ground that the Tribunal has exercised its discretion.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should have interfered with the Tribunal's order because the Tribunal's discretion was not exercised in accordance with well-settled principles.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments focused on defending the Tribunal's order, thereby implicitly arguing that the High Court was correct not to interfere with a valid exercise of discretion.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a Tribunal exercises its discretion to award reinstatement or compensation for an illegal dismissal, it must do so judicially and in accordance with well-recognized principles by examining the specific circumstances of the case. If the Tribunal exercises its discretion in disregard of such principles or circumstances, it is a failure to exercise discretion legally. In such an event, the High Court, under its writ jurisdiction, must interfere and cannot refuse to examine the case simply because the Tribunal has exercised its discretion; a failure to do so amounts to a refusal by the High Court to exercise its own jurisdiction.
obiter: While the normal rule for wrongful dismissal is reinstatement, a Tribunal has the discretion to award compensation if the circumstances are unusual or exceptional, such as when an employer's genuine loss of confidence makes reinstatement hazardous to the industry.
If a statutory tribunal exercises its discretion on the basis of irrelevant considerations or without regard to relevant considerations, certiorari may properly issue to quash its order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While reinstatement is the normal remedy for an illegal termination, it is not appropriate where an employer has a genuine, non-victimisation-based apprehension that retaining an employee would be hazardous for security reasons; in such cases, compensation is the proper remedy. The Industrial Tribunal erred by exercising its discretion 'mechanically' in ordering reinstatement without considering the employer's genuine security concerns. The High Court subsequently erred by refusing to exercise its writ jurisdiction to correct the Tribunal's flawed order, as a mechanical refusal to review an improper exercise of discretion amounts to a failure to exercise jurisdiction itself.
legal_tests_applied: When deciding between reinstatement and compensation, if a tribunal concludes from the circumstances that an employer's apprehensions about an employee are genuine and that the employer truly feels it is hazardous or prejudicial to the industry's interests to retain the workman on security grounds, the case is properly one where compensation meets the ends of justice.

A High Court can and should issue a writ of certiorari to quash an order from a statutory tribunal if that tribunal exercises its discretion on the basis of irrelevant considerations or without regard to relevant considerations, such as well-settled legal principles.

A High Court cannot refuse to interfere with a tribunal's discretionary order on the sole ground that discretion was exercised; it must examine the circumstances to ascertain whether the discretion was exercised properly and in accordance with settled principles. To do otherwise is a refusal to exercise its own jurisdiction.
policy_considerations: Courts and tribunals must attempt to reconcile the conflicting interests of the employer and the employee, balancing the employee's right to security of service against the potential for industrial disharmony that could result from imposing an unwanted workman on an unwilling employer.

To avoid prolonging disputes, which is not fair or conducive to the interests of the parties, an appellate court may decide to determine the final amount of compensation itself rather than remanding the case for further proceedings.
